description: A master's thesis or doctoral dissertation: chapters around a coherent set of contributions.
goal: Make the thesis defensible: original, substantiated, coherent across chapters and compliant with the institution's rules.
note: Units are chapters. Each chapter's claims lens checks the chapter; in every global round a cross-unit claims review builds the contribution map over the abstract, introduction, chapter summaries and conclusion, and the editor-in-chief reopens chapters that disagree. Put the introduction and conclusion chapters in a final stage so they are revised after the chapters they summarize.

readers.persona: an external thesis examiner who checks that the claimed contributions are original, substantiated and consistent across the abstract, introduction, chapters and conclusion, and prepares viva questions about the weakest points

a researcher who knows the field well; flags what is imprecise, outdated, shallow or missing (assumptions, guarantees, recent results, failure cases, open problems, key related work) and anything they would skip as already known
an intelligent nonspecialist (committee member or panel generalist) who needs the significance, the main idea and the conclusions to be clear without specialist knowledge

reviewers.focus: compliance with every applicable rule of the project's guidelines and style sheet; cite the rule for each finding

correctness of every definition, claim, derivation, equation, algorithm, number and code fragment; recompute numerical examples with a script; consistent notation, units and dimensions; correct statements of known results and their assumptions

calibration and coherence of claims: no overclaiming (unsupported superlatives, 'prove' for empirical results, 'state of the art' without dated evidence, generalizing beyond the evidence) and no underselling (stacked hedges, buried or vague contributions); every contribution stated in the abstract and introduction is supported by specific evidence in the body and restated consistently in the discussion and conclusion; limitations are honest; numbers and claims agree everywhere they appear

experimental design and reporting: research questions mapped to experiments, appropriate datasets and baselines (strong, tuned, current), ablations, statistical uncertainty (seeds, variance, confidence intervals, significance where claimed), fair comparison and compute budgets, reproducibility details, negative or mixed results reported, and conclusions drawn only from what the experiments show

every reference is real and correctly described: verify authors, title, venue, year and identifier (DOI, arXiv id, ISBN or publisher page) with web search and the citation checker; flag any reference that cannot be found as a blocker; check that each cited work actually supports the sentence citing it, that primary sources are cited, and that essential related work is not missing

the rendered document: figures, tables, equations, algorithms, lists, headings and layout; legibility at print size, labels and units, captions that say what to notice, every figure and table referred to and explained in the text

fluency and coherence: paragraph flow and transitions, one idea per paragraph, consistent terminology, no repetitive wording or formulaic transitions, the house rules (no en or em dashes, only needed hyphens, no comma right after a conjunction or connective, no paragraph opening with 'To', every abbreviation written out at first use and none in the abstract, no internal identifiers such as function names, versions or hashes), no chains of 'and', parallel lists, sentence variety, concision, and American or British spelling used consistently as configured

editors.focus: prose: clarity, concision, flow between sentences and paragraphs, terminology, punctuation including hyphens and dashes, parallel lists; remove filler, formulaic transitions and repetition without removing substance or adding claims

notation, terminology and spelling across the document and against the glossary; numbers, names and claims identical wherever repeated (abstract, introduction, body, conclusion); labels, cross-references, captions, citation and reference formatting
